account: A 72-year-old man's right arm was replanted at Sahlgrenska University Hospital in Mölndal, Sweden, after a traumatic above-elbow amputation. He had no functional recovery after conventional rehabilitation and developed chronic neuropathic pain. A team from the Center for Bionics and Pain Research and Sahlgrenska University Hospital (C.A.R.E.), based in Mölndal, then delivered 18 sessions of myoelectric motor execution over 84 days. The paper does not name the treatment site. Nine of the sessions included sensory training with tactile grids. A linear discriminant analysis classifier (Neuromotus, Integrum AB) classified eight channels of electromyography. It decoded intended movements from the replanted arm, and a screen showed them as virtual limbs and games. He regained active thumb extension (4 degrees) and active wrist flexion (6 degrees) and extension (10 degrees), movements absent before treatment. Pain fluctuated with no consistent change. The paper reports no follow-up after the final session. Treatment dates are not given. The authors first posted the case as a preprint on 15 January 2024, after the treatment had ended, and the case is dated to that preprint. The journal published the paper on 23 November 2024. The two papers that cite it by October 2026 both list Ortiz-Catalan as an author.

ai_role.statement: The LDA classifier decodes intended movements from weak EMG in a hand and wrist with no active motion. That is the only way the patient could receive real-time feedback on his motor attempts. The authors attribute the regained movement to this motor execution training. Two authors hold a pending patent on the technology.

fields.headline: Man regains thumb and wrist movement in a paralyzed replanted arm
fields.title: Machine-learning myoelectric motor execution partially restores thumb and wrist movement in a paralyzed replanted arm

provenance.basis: SHA-256 of the public case, its assessments, and its displayed answers and notes, excluding its own identifier and the derived coverage summary.

value.role: SHA-256 of the complete public case and its assessments

fields.account: A 72-year-old man's right arm was replanted at Sahlgrenska University Hospital in Mölndal, Sweden, after a traumatic above-elbow amputation. He had no functional recovery after conventional rehabilitation and developed chronic neuropathic pain. A team from the Center for Bionics and Pain Research and Sahlgrenska University Hospital (C.A.R.E.), based in Mölndal, then delivered 18 sessions of myoelectric motor execution over 84 days. The paper does not name the treatment site. Nine of the sessions included sensory training with tactile grids. A linear discriminant analysis classifier (Neuromotus, Integrum AB) classified eight channels of electromyography. It decoded intended movements from the replanted arm, and a screen showed them as virtual limbs and games. He regained active thumb extension (4 degrees) and active wrist flexion (6 degrees) and extension (10 degrees), movements absent before treatment. Pain fluctuated with no consistent change. The paper reports no follow-up after the final session. Treatment dates are not given. The authors first posted the case as a preprint on 15 January 2024, after the treatment had ended, and the case is dated to that preprint. The journal published the paper on 23 November 2024. The two papers that cite it by October 2026 both list Ortiz-Catalan as an author.

produced_by: Residual EMG detectable in the impaired limb
Classifier trained on the patient's own signals each session
Repeated sessions with virtual-limb and game feedback

purpose: Rehabilitate a highly impaired replanted arm and reduce neuropathic pain using decoded motor intention as feedback

ratings.reason: The patient regained active thumb and wrist movement that conventional rehabilitation had not produced. The gains are small, and pain did not consistently improve.
The paper reports a single case with no follow-up and no use beyond the treating group, so no realized societal outcome is documented.

revisions.change: Record drafted from the cited sources.

Reworded the account and deployer so that Sahlgrenska University Hospital is credited only with the replantation surgery because the paper never says where the MME sessions were delivered; corrected the article numbers to 21:204 and 22:6; qualified the title and the system's part to “partially restores” and “a hand and wrist with no active motion” to match the paper's own limits; and restored the full source title on evidence 2.
